presentingComplaint: Sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness at rest
history: Tall, thin, previously well non-athletic man who developed abrupt right-sided sharp chest pain radiating to the shoulder while sitting quietly, immediately followed by mild breathlessness. No preceding trauma, exertion, cough, fever or infective symptoms. Long-standing smoker (10 pack-years); no known lung disease, asthma or connective-tissue disorder. No prior similar episodes. No calf pain, immobilisation or recent travel.
examination: Comfortable at rest but mildly tachypnoeic. Trachea central. Reduced chest expansion on the right with hyper-resonant percussion note and diminished/absent breath sounds over the right hemithorax; reduced tactile vocal fremitus. No tracheal deviation, no raised JVP, no distended neck veins (no tension features). Left lung clear. Calves soft and non-tender; no leg swelling. Marfanoid habitus (tall, slim).

labs.ECG: Sinus rhythm, no ischaemic changes, no S1Q3T3
labs.D-dimer: Not indicated (low pre-test probability of PE)

imaging: Erect PA chest radiograph: visible visceral pleural line on the right with absence of lung markings peripheral to it; estimated rim of air ~2.5 cm at the hilum (large per BTS). No mediastinal shift, no fluid level, no underlying parenchymal disease. Lung point confirmed on bedside thoracic ultrasound (absent lung sliding with barcode sign).
differentialDiagnoses: Acute coronary syndrome / musculoskeletal chest pain
contraindications: Avoid positive-pressure ventilation / air travel and diving until resolved (risk of tension pneumothorax)
Needle/tube insertion caveat in coagulopathy or anticoagulation
edgeCases: Progression to tension pneumothorax with hypotension, tracheal deviation and distended neck veins — decompress immediately, do not wait for imaging
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in older smokers/COPD behaves more severely at smaller sizes
expectedMaiK: Sudden pleuritic chest pain with unilateral hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds in a tall young smoker is classic for a spontaneous pneumothorax; confirm with erect chest X-ray and watch for tension features which mandate immediate needle decompression.
expectedNextQuestions: Any tracheal deviation, hypotension or distended neck veins to suggest tension?
Any preceding trauma, and is there a history of prior pneumothorax or underlying lung disease?
expectedInvestigations: Bedside thoracic ultrasound / point-of-care assessment for lung sliding
